SGP Criticism

 • SGPs are unreliable
 o Using the same or similar dataset of student results, consistent
 SGPs are calculated
 o SGP error is modeled from random and non-random error in testing
 • There is no validity evidence to support the use of SGPs
 o Use of SGPs in mode-adjusted studies (MA DESE, in publication)
 • SGPs violate Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing
 o Advice encourages descriptive use of SGPs, not intended for
 generating teacher evaluation results

 From: Sireci, S. G., Wells, C. S., & Keller, L. A. (2016). Why we should abandon student
 growth percentiles.

SGP Computation

 • Computed using an R routine:
 o Quantile Regression generates 100 regression lines where
 students are assigned a SGP from 1 to 99
 o All students are used in the analysis – there is no “small N”
 problem regarding cohorts (cohorts are a way to explain the
 estimation using prior performance, but that is not exactly
 the way SGPs are calculated)
 o B-Spline smoothing to provide better fit at the end of the
 distributions
 o Distribution of the SGPs is largely uniform with slightly more
 enrollments in the 1st and 99th quantiles

Modeling SGP Error

 • SGP SEMs are calculation using scaled score CSEMs
 provided as part of the state’s assessment data used for
 SGP calculation.
 • Scale scored CSEMs are used to perturb the observed
 scales so that 100 simulated SGPs are calculated for
 each student.
 • The 100 simulated SGPs are used to calculate a standard
 error for each SGP reported.
 • In general, state assessment systems show standard
 errors for SGPs between 5 and 15.
4/23/19

Modeling SGP Error

 • SGPs, being percentiles, are uniformly distributed.
 • However, the distribution of observed SGPs based
 upon a normal CSEM is normal.
 • That is, a for a student with a true SGP of 50,
 observed SGPs occur most often near 50.
 • For example, a student with an SGP a true SGP of 50,
 would expect to see an observed SGP of 20 or less
 2.5% of the time (assuming an SGP SEM of 15).

Modeling SGP Error

 • In situations where students demonstrate low growth
 (e.g., SGP <= 20), the chances of them having true
 growth >= 50 (the dividing line for demonstrating a
 year’s growth) is < 2%.
 • Because SGPs are uniformly distributed, 20% of
 students have SGPs <= 20.
 • Using low SGPs as a flag for investigation of students in
 possible need of remediation would be justified as those
 students likely didn’t demonstrate a year’s worth of
 growth.

AGGREGATED SGPS

SGPs in Aggregations

 • Properties of SGPs different for student-level and for
 aggregated levels
 • SGPs provide key information about student progress
 • SGPs are much less correlated with student
 demographic data than achievement scores
 • At the student level, allow for near-equal opportunity to
 grow
 o However, it is important to understand that students are not
 randomly assigned; consequently, low-growing students are
 somewhat more likely in certain situations than others

INFORMATION FOR GUIDANCE MATERIALS

Reporting Recommendations
 1. Use SGP reports to enhance instructional/curricular planning
 2. Report SGPs alongside contextual information (courses,
 grades, etc.)
 3. SGPs should be reported alongside information on prior
 (baseline) achievement to enhance appropriate interpretations
 4. Reporting multiple years of SGPs will reduce spurious decisions
 5. At the aggregated levels of reporting, filters may improve the
 interpretation of SGPs
 6. At the aggregated levels, the range of low, moderate, and high
 SGPs should be adjusted according to the distributions
